facts.text: Idomeneo was a commission: in 1780 the Elector of Bavaria, Karl Theodor, asked Mozart and librettist Varesco for an opera for the Munich court carnival.
facts.evidence: Mozart and Varesco were commissioned in 1780 by Karl Theodor, Elector of Bavaria for a court carnival.

facts.text: Listen to the end of the overture: its soft final chords are not a real ending but lead straight into G minor, the key of Ilia’s opening scene.
facts.evidence: turn out not to be a resolution of the overture in the tonic but chords in the dominant of G minor

facts.text: The opera premiered on 29 January 1781 at the Cuvilliés Theatre in Munich, conducted by Christian Cannabich.
evidence: It was first performed at the Cuvilliés Theatre of the Munich Residenz on 29 January 1781, under the musical direction of Christian Cannabich.

facts.text: The Munich press notice of the premiere didn’t mention Mozart by name. It raved about the sets instead, especially the view of the port and Neptune’s temple.
evidence: a notice in the Munich press did not mention Mozart by name
the view of the port and Neptune's temple were outstanding

facts.text: Idamante was written for a castrato. For a 1786 concert performance in Vienna, Mozart rewrote the part for a tenor.
evidence: A concert performance was given in 1786 at the Palais Auersperg in Vienna.
changed Idamante from a castrato to a tenor

facts.text: Mozart fought with his librettist, the court chaplain Varesco, making big cuts and even changing words whose vowels the singers disliked, like the many i’s in “rinvigorir”.
facts.evidence: Mozart fought with the librettist, the court chaplain Varesco, making large cuts and changes, even down to specific words and vowels disliked by the singers

facts.text: Elettra’s “Tutte nel cor vi sento”: jealous of Ilia, she feels the furies of the underworld rising up in her heart.
facts.evidence: feels the furies of the underworld rise up in her heart

facts.text: This shipwreck scene closely follows the structure of a similar storm scene in Gluck’s Iphigénie en Tauride.
facts.evidence: the shipwreck scene towards the end of act 1 is almost identical to the structure and dramatic working-out of a similar scene in Gluck's Iphigénie en Tauride

facts.text: Saved from the storm, Idomeneo remembers his vow to Neptune: to sacrifice the first living creature he meets on land. It will be his own son.
facts.evidence: to sacrifice, if he should arrive safely on land, the first living creature he should meet

facts.text: Mozart wrote the title role for the tenor Anton Raaff, who sang it at the 1781 premiere. It was Raaff’s last stage role.
evidence: Raaff sang the title role in the premiere of Mozart's 1781 opera Idomeneo; this was his last stage role.

facts.text: The critic Schubart thought Anton Raaff, the first Idomeneo, had the most beautiful male voice of all time.
facts.attribution: C. F. D. Schubart (via Wikipedia, “Anton Raaff”)
facts.evidence: In the opinion of Schubart, his was the most beautiful male voice of all time

facts.text: In this intermezzo between Acts I and II, Cretan troops come off Idomeneo’s ship, their wives meet them, and everyone praises Neptune.
facts.evidence: In an intermezzo between acts 1 and 2, Cretan troops disembarking from Idomeneo's ship are met by their wives, and all praise Neptune.

facts.text: Mozart saves the piccolo for this one place in the opera: the storm in Act II.
facts.evidence: piccolo (only in the storm of act 2)

facts.text: “Zeffiretti lusinghieri”: alone in the royal garden, Ilia asks the breezes to carry her love to Idamante.
facts.evidence: Ilia asks the breezes to carry her love to Idamante

facts.text: The three trombones play only here, to accompany the offstage Voice of Neptune.
facts.evidence: 3 trombones (only accompanying the off-stage voice of Neptune in act 3)

facts.text: Idomeneo was the first opera in which Mozart ended in the key of the overture, and he did so in all his later operas.
facts.evidence: ended the work in the key of the overture

facts.text: Despite all that work, Idomeneo was performed only three times in Munich.
facts.evidence: Idomeneo was performed three times in Munich.

facts.text: Mozart also wrote about 15 minutes of ballet music (K. 367) for Idomeneo, which the Munich management requested. He reported on it in a letter to his father on 30 December 1780.
evidence: he reported in a letter to his father of 30 December 1780
It is in several parts and lasts around fifteen minutes.

facts.text: Later in 1781 Mozart considered making the opera more like Gluck, with a bass Idomeneo and a tenor Idamante, but he never did.
facts.evidence: this would have meant a bass Idomeneo and a tenor Idamante

facts.text: For the 150th anniversary in 1931, Richard Strauss made his own version for Vienna, replacing about a third of Mozart’s score with his own music.
evidence: the Vienna State Opera presented a distinctively interventionist version of the score by Richard Strauss
Strauss replaced about 1/3 of Mozart's score with some of his own music

facts.text: The first US performance came only in 1947, at Tanglewood, produced by Boris Goldovsky.
facts.evidence: The first performance in the United States was produced by Boris Goldovsky at the Berkshire Music Festival at Tanglewood during the summer of 1947.

facts.text: In 2006 the Deutsche Oper Berlin cancelled a revival of Hans Neuenfels’s Idomeneo, citing an “incalculable security risk” over its added final scene.
evidence: the Deutsche Oper Berlin announced the cancellation of four performances

facts.text: This Jean-Pierre Ponnelle staging was the Met’s first production of Idomeneo. It opened on October 14, 1982, with Luciano Pavarotti in the title role.
facts.attribution: Met Opera Archives, performance record CID 270240

facts.text: Ponnelle framed the stage with classical Roman columns and a broad flight of steps, in front of changing backdrops of ruins inspired by Piranesi.
facts.attribution: F. Warren O’Reilly, Washington Times, 1982 (Met Opera Archives)
evidence: Ponnelle's use of classical Roman columns framing the stage, a broad flight of steps between

facts.text: At the Met premiere, a critic wrote that Hildegard Behrens as Elettra “literally stopped the show” with this last-act aria.
facts.attribution: F. Warren O’Reilly, Washington Times, 1982 (Met Opera Archives)
facts.evidence: Hildegard Behrens as Elettra, thrwarted in her efforts to win Idamante from Ilia, literally stopped the show with her brilliant last act aria

facts.text: The 1982 Washington Times review praised the opera’s two storm sequences, which it called perhaps the first realistic musical tempests in any opera.
facts.attribution: F. Warren O’Reilly, Washington Times, 1982 (Met Opera Archives)
evidence: two magnificent sequences of storm music, thought bo be the first such realistic musical tempests in any opera
